introduction-when-npm-run-build-isnt-eno.core: Simple build commands rebuild everything and depend on the machine they run on. At monorepo scale you need hermetic builds, a dependency graph to rebuild only what changed, and shared caching and execution.

first_principles.problem: A 4-hour full build across 500 engineers means nobody gets fast feedback, and results differ between laptops and CI.
truths: Most changes affect a small part of the code.
Repeated work across engineers is waste.

analogy.title: A city kitchen cooking for millions
analogy.story: You can't re-cook every dish when one recipe changes; you track which dishes use which ingredient.
analogy.breaks: These tools (Bazel, Buck2) have a steep adoption cost. Smaller repos may not need them.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Feedback goes from hours to minutes.

check.q: Why can't simple build scripts scale to huge monorepos?
check.a: They rebuild everything and have implicit inputs, so they're slow and non-deterministic.

the-core-principle-hermetic-builds.core: A hermetic build uses only explicitly declared inputs (pinned toolchains, dependencies, sources) and is isolated from the host's environment, network and installed software.

first_principles.problem: Builds silently use whatever compiler, library or env var happens to be on the machine.
derivation: **Sandbox** actions so they see only the declared inputs.

analogy.title: Baking in a sealed room with a measured kit
analogy.story: Not 'flour from the pantry and tap water', but exactly these sealed ingredients, in a room where nothing else can get in.
analogy.breaks: Perfect hermeticity is hard. Timestamps and some tools leak non-determinism.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The build sees only these sources and pinned deps.

example.outcome: builds that don't depend on the machine.

check.a: Relying on undeclared inputs like host-installed tools, env vars or network fetches.

the-benefit-of-hermeticity-determinism.core: Hermeticity gives determinism: the same inputs always produce bit-identical outputs on any machine. That makes builds reproducible, debuggable and cacheable.

first_principles.problem: 'Works on my machine' bugs and CI failures that nobody can reproduce locally waste days.
truths: The same function with the same inputs gives the same output.
Reproducibility is also a security property.
derivation: Use it to enable **caching** and **reproducible releases**.

analogy.title: A calculator
analogy.story: 2+2 gives 4 on every calculator in the world. A build should behave the same way.
analogy.breaks: Floating-point and parallel ordering can still introduce subtle variation.

check.q: Why is determinism a prerequisite for remote caching?
check.a: Outputs can only be reused safely if the same inputs are guaranteed to produce the same outputs.

monorepo-tooling-the-dependency-graph.core: Build tools model the codebase as a graph of targets and their dependencies. A change rebuilds and retests only the affected targets (the changed node and its dependents), not the whole repo.

first_principles.problem: Rebuilding everything for a one-line change wastes hours for every engineer.
truths: Most targets don't depend on a given change.
derivation: Enforce **visibility** to keep the graph clean.

analogy.title: A subway map
analogy.story: A closure on one line only affects the stations downstream on it, not the whole network.
analogy.breaks: Undeclared dependencies break the model, which is why hermeticity matters.

example.title: Querying affected targets
example.outcome: CI time scales with the size of the change, not the repo.

check.q: What determines which targets need rebuilding after a change?
check.a: The changed targets plus everything that transitively depends on them.

remote-caching-dont-do-the-same-work-twi.core: Because outputs are a pure function of their inputs, each build action is keyed by the hash of its inputs. Before running it, check a shared remote cache: if anyone has already built it, download the result instead.

first_principles.problem: 500 engineers and CI all compile the same unchanged libraries again and again.
derivation: Compute the **action key** = hash(inputs, command, env).
**Look up** the key in the remote cache (CAS).

analogy.title: A shared answer book for maths homework
analogy.story: If someone has already solved exactly this problem, you copy the verified answer.
analogy.breaks: Cache poisoning is a risk if untrusted machines can write, so restrict writes.

example.title: A fresh laptop build

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Nobody repeats work someone else has already done.

example.outcome: builds approach the cost of the true change.

check.q: What is a remote cache keyed on?
check.a: A hash of all inputs to a build action (files, command and environment).

remote-execution-infinite-compute-power.core: Remote execution sends build actions to a farm of workers, so thousands run in parallel and builds aren't limited to a laptop's 16 cores. Hermeticity makes this safe.

first_principles.problem: Even with caching, a large genuine change takes an hour on one machine.
truths: Independent actions can run anywhere in parallel.
Hermetic actions behave the same on any worker.
Clusters have far more cores than laptops.
derivation: Workers fetch inputs from the **CAS**, execute and upload outputs.
Parallelism is limited only by **graph width**.

analogy.title: Outsourcing to a thousand cooks
analogy.story: Instead of one chef cooking 1,000 dishes, you send each order to a huge kitchen that cooks them all at once.
analogy.breaks: Network transfer of inputs can dominate for small actions, so tune it.

example.title: Compiling 5,000 C++ files

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Big changes get fast feedback too.

example.outcome: build speed scales with compute, not laptops.

check.q: Why does remote execution require hermetic builds?
check.a: Actions must produce identical results on any worker, using only declared inputs.

putting-it-all-together-the-build-system.core: The build stack is layered: hermeticity gives determinism, determinism enables a precise dependency graph and safe caching, and caching plus remote execution make builds fast at any scale.

first_principles.problem: Teams adopt remote caching without hermeticity and get wrong results, or a graph without caching and still get slow builds.
truths: Each layer depends on the one below.
Skipping a layer undermines the ones above it.

analogy.title: A building's floors
analogy.story: You can't build the penthouse (remote execution) without the foundation (hermeticity).
analogy.breaks: Adoption is incremental. Start with hermeticity in critical paths.

example.title: A monorepo migration roadmap
example.outcome: a build system that scales with growth.

check.q: Why can't you safely add remote caching to a non-hermetic build?
check.a: Undeclared inputs mean the same cache key could correspond to different outputs, giving wrong results.
